content:
This section is not a continuous argument but the end of the book's main text followed by its Notes apparatus. File page 326 closes the body with Steven Pinker's discussion of philosophical puzzles; file pages 327 through 338 are endnotes keyed to printed page numbers, so the printed labels visible here (roughly 565 through 576) belong to the notes, not to the argument.

Source claims. On file page 326, Pinker argues that scientific theories succeed because they use words, equations and computer simulations — combinatorial media matching how minds work — and because parts of the world are lawful interactions among simpler elements. Philosophy's hard problems resist this treatment: sentience is not obviously a combination of brain or computational states, the "I" is a unity over time located nowhere in particular, free will is by definition not a causal chain, and the core act of referring remains a puzzle even though the combinatorics of meaning (how words form sentence meanings) is worked out. Knowledge also puzzles because knowers grasp things never experienced. He conjectures these enigmas may stem from a mismatch between the problems and the combinatorial apparatus natural selection gave us, and closes that our bafflement may be the price of a mind able to build languages, theories, poems and stories (file page 326).

The notes supply pointers rather than arguments, but they map the book's relevant terrain. Representation and generalization, multiple representations, mental imagery, memory chunks and "mentalese" are cited at printed pages 86–90 (file pages 330–331). Perception as inverse optics, description, and probabilistic inference appears at printed pages 28–29 and 212–249 (file pages 328, 337–338), including stereo vision, shading, and "betting on a regular world." Learning's dependence on innate mechanism is flagged at printed page 33 (file page 328). Compositionality and systematicity, propositions in networks, amnesic networks, fuzzy categories and explanation-based generalization appear at printed pages 120–128 (file pages 332–333). Time and memory are touched by recurrent networks, short-term loops and multiple memory systems (printed pages 90, 123–125; file pages 330–332). Goals, causation and social cognition surface in notes on beliefs and desires (printed page 64), animal navigation and conditioning as time-series analysis (printed pages 179–182), primate social intelligence and cognitive arms races (printed pages 193–194), and emotional coloring of memory (printed page 143) (file pages 330, 335–336, 333). Analogy and creativity are not developed here; only adjacent topics such as exaptation and vision co-opted for abstract concepts appear (printed pages 171, 191; file pages 335–336).

Limits and disagreements are explicit in the note headings: problems with perceptrons and connectoplasm, failure of recurrent networks to handle propositions, problems with fuzzy categories, amnesic networks, and debates over the past tense (printed pages 109–127; file pages 331–332). The Chinese Room and Penrose draw refutations (printed pages 93–97; file page 331). Innate versus acquired is distinguished at printed pages 33 and 238–240, where prewired stereo circuitry coexists with experience-dependent sharpening (file pages 328, 338). The past-tense debate is a narrow language-learning dispute, not a universal learning law (printed page 112; file page 331).

Engineering implications, clearly separated: the notes suggest a machine needs explicit structured representations with variable binding and systematic recombination, plus constraint-based perceptual inference that treats vision as an ill-posed problem resolved by world regularities, and memory systems that separate fast learning from consolidation to avoid catastrophic interference. Permitted scope of a rule must be represented compositionally, not memorized as a list of cases. None of this demonstrates human intelligence or consciousness; the source itself says the subjective feel and reference remain unexplained (file page 326). Uncertainty: some note text is garbled or OCR-damaged (for example "Fbdor," "Sovvell," "Stereogratn"), and page numbers cited are the notes' printed targets, not file pages.
